definition: Canny means shrewd and careful in practical matters.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word canny. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know canny should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The canny landlady rents the ground floor to a bakery at a discount — the smell of warm bread has sold every unit upstairs.
A sensible buyer avoids the obvious mistakes; a canny one goes further, reading angles and timing that most people never notice.
Crafty goes past canny into tricks and misdirection — the canny operator plays the odds sharply but plays them fair.

Shrewd praises sharp judgment — a shrewd reader of people and situations sees the angle others miss. Canny takes that sharpness and adds a careful, self-protecting streak: it hedges, risks little, and quietly banks the advantage. A shrewd move can be bold; a canny one rarely is.

Savvy is insider fluency — the practical know-how you earn from years inside one particular scene or trade, the way a roadie or a day trader knows their world. Canny needs no résumé: it is careful, sharp-eyed practical judgment that travels, working in situations its owner has never met before.

Rosa's food truck skips the county fair every year.
The pitch fees there eat a week's profit, so instead she parks at the marathon finish line, where four thousand hungry runners funnel past exactly one vendor.
She studies foot-traffic maps in January the way other cooks study recipes.
Nothing about the plan is flashy; all of it is canny, and all of it works.
Canny is the exact word for Rosa because it means shrewd and careful in practical matters — judgment applied where money, timing, and people actually move.
A brilliant cook might still choose the wrong corner.
The canny one reads the situation first, risks little, and quietly comes out ahead.

At estate sales, Ruta never heads for the bookshelves first.
She lingers by the kitchen boxes, buys a few jars, and listens to which dealers are sighing over the library.
Only near closing, when the sighing dealers have talked each other into overpaying for the famous titles, does she drift over and make one canny offer — for the boxes nobody sorted.
She caps what she will spend before she walks in, and she has never once broken the cap.
Twice a year, an unsorted box turns out to hold a signed first edition, and that pays for every jar of buttons she will never use.
